title: Τέρας καὶ Νέστωρ
titleEn: The Omen of the Sparrows and Nestor’s Rebuke — Iliad 2.278–368
part: The Omen of the Sparrows and Nestor’s Rebuke (2.278–368)
about: Athena, made like a herald, hushes the army, and Odysseus stands with the sceptre. He tells Agamemnon that the soldiers are shaming him by wanting to go home, grants that nine years is hard, and asks them to hold out. He recalls the omen at Aulis: a serpent sent by Zeus devoured a sparrow’s eight nestlings and then their mother, and was turned to stone. Calchas read it as nine years of war and Troy taken in the tenth. The army roars its approval. Nestor then scolds the assembly as children, tells Agamemnon to lead, to let the quitters waste away, and to sort the men by tribes and clans, so that he will learn who is base and whether the gods or men are to blame.

sentences.t: ὣς φάσαν ἣ πληθύς·
sentences.l: So they spoke, the multitude;
sentences.i: So the multitude spoke;
sentences.n: The unnamed soldiers have just finished praising Odysseus (2.272–277), and ‘they’ here is the whole army. φάσαν is ἔφασαν ‘they said’, unaugmented, an ordinary Homeric past tense. ἣ πληθύς is ‘she, the multitude’: in Homer the ‘article’ is a pronoun, and ἣ, its feminine form, stands with the noun that names the speakers.

sentences.t:
ἀνὰ δ’ ὃ πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἔστη σκῆπτρον ἔχων·
sentences.l:
and up he, the city-sacking Odysseus,
stood, holding the sceptre;
sentences.i: Then Odysseus, the city-sacker, stood up, holding the sceptre;
sentences.n: ἀνὰ … ἔστη is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb: ἀνέστη ‘stood up’. ὃ is the old demonstrative ‘he’, with Ὀδυσσεύς and its epithet beside it. πτολίπορθος ‘city-sacking’ (πτόλις, the epic form of πόλις, and πέρθω ‘sack’) is the stock epithet of Odysseus, translated every time. The sceptre is Agamemnon’s, which he took at 2.185–186; ἔστη σκῆπτρον ἔχων also describes Agamemnon at 2.101.

sentences.t:
παρὰ δὲ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
εἰδομένη κήρυκι σιωπᾶν λαὸν ἀνώγει,
ὡς ἅμα θ’ οἳ πρῶτοί τε καὶ ὕστατοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
μῦθον ἀκούσειαν καὶ ἐπιφρασσαίατο βουλήν·
sentences.l:
and beside him gleaming-eyed Athena,
having made herself like a herald, bade the people be silent,
so that together both the first and the last, the sons of the Achaeans,
might hear the speech and take note of the plan:
sentences.i: and beside him gleaming-eyed Athena, made like a herald, bade the people be silent, so that the first and the last of the sons of the Achaeans might hear the speech together and take note of the plan:
sentences.n: This is the Athena who sent Odysseus out at 2.166–181. εἰδομένη κήρυκι is ‘having made herself like a herald’ (εἴδομαι with the dative), so the soldiers hear a herald’s call for silence. ἀνώγει ‘bade’ takes the infinitive σιωπᾶν ‘to be silent’. ὡς with the optatives ἀκούσειαν and ἐπιφρασσαίατο is purpose: ‘so that they might hear … and take note of’. ἅμα θ’ … πρῶτοί τε καὶ ὕστατοι is ‘both first and last, together’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: The speech-introducing line, as at 1.73, 1.253 and 2.78; the Odyssey has it as well. ὅ is ‘he’, Odysseus, and σφιν ‘to them’. ἐὺ φρονέων ‘thinking well’ is rendered ‘with kindly intent’ every time, even when, as here, the speech that follows is hard. ἀγορήσατο ‘addressed the assembly’ and μετέειπεν ‘spoke among them’ are aorists.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη νῦν δή σε ἄναξ ἐθέλουσιν Ἀχαιοὶ
πᾶσιν ἐλέγχιστον θέμεναι μερόπεσσι βροτοῖσιν,
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, now indeed, lord, the Achaeans wish
to make you most shameful for all speech-dividing mortals,
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, now indeed, lord, the Achaeans wish to make you most shameful to all mortals of articulate speech,
sentences.n: Odysseus begins by telling Agamemnon that, after the rush for the ships, the army is shaming him. ἄναξ is the vocative, ‘lord’. ἐλέγχιστον is the superlative of ἐλεγχής ‘shameful’; θέμεναι, the aorist infinitive of τίθημι with the epic ending -μεναι, takes two accusatives, ‘make you most shameful’. μερόπεσσι βροτοῖσιν: the meaning of μέροπες is not known; the ancient explanation ‘speech-dividing’, that is ‘of articulate speech’, is followed. The edition prints no quotation marks; the English adds them.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τοι ἐκτελέουσιν ὑπόσχεσιν ἥν περ ὑπέσταν
ἐνθάδ’ ἔτι στείχοντες ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο
Ἴλιον ἐκπέρσαντ’ εὐτείχεον ἀπονέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and not for you do they fulfil the promise which they undertook
hither, still going from Argos, horse-pasturing,
Ilios, well-walled, having sacked-utterly, to return home.
sentences.i: and they are not fulfilling for you the promise they undertook, when they were still on their way here from horse-pasturing Argos, to sack well-walled Ilios and return home.
sentences.n: ὑπόσχεσιν ἥν περ ὑπέσταν is ‘the promise which they undertook’: ὑπέσταν is ὑπέστησαν, the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι ‘undertake’, in its epic short form. τοι is read as ‘to you’ (σοι), though it could be the particle. ἐκτελέουσιν is the uncontracted ἐκτελοῦσιν ‘they carry out’ (the form could also be a future, ‘will carry out’; the English takes the present). ἱπποβότοιο ‘horse-pasturing’ is the stock epithet of Argos. The last line is word for word 2.113, where Agamemnon says Zeus promised it; here it is what the army undertook.

sentences.t:
ὥς τε γὰρ ἢ παῖδες νεαροὶ χῆραί τε γυναῖκες
ἀλλήλοισιν ὀδύρονται οἶκον δὲ νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
For like children, young ones, or widowed women
to one another they lament about going home.
sentences.i: For like young children or widowed women they lament to one another about going home.
sentences.n: Odysseus likens the army to the weakest people he can name. ὥς τε is ‘just as’; ἢ is taken as ‘or’. παῖδες νεαροί ‘young children’, χῆραι γυναῖκες ‘widowed women’. ὀδύρονται ‘they lament’ is followed by an infinitive, so the lament is about going home. οἶκον δέ is printed as two words: δέ is the suffix -δε of direction (‘homeward’), not ‘and’. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted νεῖσθαι ‘to go’.

sentences.t: ἦ μὴν καὶ πόνος ἐστὶν ἀνιηθέντα νέεσθαι·
sentences.l: Truly, there is also toil, to go home distressed;
sentences.i: Truly it is a toil, too, to go home distressed;
sentences.n: Odysseus grants the soldiers their grievance before he answers it. ἦ μήν is ‘truly’. πόνος ἐστί with an infinitive is ‘it is a toil to…’. ἀνιηθέντα is the aorist passive participle of ἀνιάω ‘distress, vex’, in the accusative to agree with the unstated subject of νέεσθαι: ‘to go home having been distressed’. πόνος is ‘toil’, as in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ τίς θ’ ἕνα μῆνα μένων ἀπὸ ἧς ἀλόχοιο
ἀσχαλάᾳ σὺν νηῒ πολυζύγῳ, ὅν περ ἄελλαι
χειμέριαι εἰλέωσιν ὀρινομένη τε θάλασσα·
sentences.i: For even a man who stays a single month away from his own wife chafes with his many-benched ship, one whom wintry storms hem in, and a stirred-up sea;
sentences.n: A month away from home is hard; Odysseus is about to say what nine years must be. τίς θ’: epic τε marks a general truth. ἧς ἀλόχοιο: ἧς is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and ἀλόχοιο the epic genitive of ἄλοχος ‘wife’. ἀσχαλάᾳ is ἀσχαλᾷ ‘chafes’ (epic diectasis). πολυζύγῳ is ‘many-yoked’ in the literal layer and ‘many-benched’ in the English: ζυγόν is the rowers’ cross-bench as well as a yoke (compare ἐϋσσέλμοιο ‘well-benched’). ὅν is masculine, so it is the man, not the feminine ship. ἄελλαι ‘blasts’ (here ‘storms’), εἰλέωσιν is a subjunctive (a general relative clause), from εἰλέω, a form of εἴλω ‘hem in’.

sentences.t:
ἡμῖν δ’ εἴνατός ἐστι περιτροπέων ἐνιαυτὸς
ἐνθάδε μιμνόντεσσι·
sentences.l:
but for us ninth is the year, as it comes round,
here, for us who stay;
sentences.i: But for us, who stay here, it is the ninth year as it comes round;
sentences.n: ἡμῖν … μιμνόντεσσι is ‘to us … who stay’, a dative participle (μίμνω is the epic form of μένω, and -εσσι the epic dative plural ending). εἴνατος is ἔνατος ‘ninth’. περιτροπέων, a participle formed on περιτρέπω ‘turn round’, is said of the year ‘as it comes round’. Odysseus sets the ninth year beside the nine birds of the omen he is about to tell.

sentences.t:
τὼ οὐ νεμεσίζομ’ Ἀχαιοὺς
ἀσχαλάαν παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν·
sentences.l:
therefore I do not feel resentment at the Achaeans
for chafing beside their curved ships;
sentences.i: So I feel no resentment at the Achaeans for chafing beside their curved ships;
sentences.n: τὼ is τῷ ‘therefore’. νεμεσίζομαι is the verb of νέμεσις, close to νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment’; it takes the accusative of the person and an infinitive: ‘I feel no resentment at the Achaeans for chafing’, that is, I do not blame them. ἀσχαλάαν is the uncontracted infinitive of the verb at 293. νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν ‘curved ships’ (κορωνίς ‘curved’).

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔμπης
αἰσχρόν τοι δηρόν τε μένειν κενεόν τε νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
but even so
shameful, indeed, both long to stay and empty to return.
sentences.i: yet even so it is shameful to stay so long and to go home empty-handed.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔμπης ‘but even so’ turns from the army’s side to the other. αἰσχρόν is ‘shameful’, a different word from ἐλέγχιστον at 285. τοι is the particle ‘you see’. δηρόν is a neuter adverb ‘for long’. κενεόν is the epic uncontracted κενόν, accusative, agreeing with the unstated subject of νέεσθαι: ‘to go back empty’, that is, empty-handed.

sentences.t:
τλῆτε φίλοι, καὶ μείνατ’ ἐπὶ χρόνον ὄφρα δαῶμεν
ἢ ἐτεὸν Κάλχας μαντεύεται ἦε καὶ οὐκί.
sentences.l:
Endure, friends, and stay for a time, until we learn
whether truly Calchas prophesies, or not.
sentences.i: Endure, friends, and stay a while, until we learn whether Calchas truly prophesies or not.
sentences.n: τλῆτε is the plural aorist imperative of τλάω ‘endure’; μείνατ’ is the aorist imperative of μένω ‘stay’, with ἐπὶ χρόνον ‘for a time’. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive δαῶμεν (δάω, an epic verb ‘learn’) means ‘until we learn’. ἢ ἐτεόν … ἦε καὶ οὐκί is a double question, ‘whether truly … or not’, ἐτεόν being an adverb ‘truly’. Calchas is the seer of 1.69–72.

sentences.t:
εὖ γὰρ δὴ τόδε ἴδμεν ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἐστὲ δὲ πάντες
μάρτυροι, οὓς μὴ κῆρες ἔβαν θανάτοιο φέρουσαι·
sentences.l:
For well indeed we know this in our minds, and you are all
witnesses, whom the death-spirits did not go bearing off:
sentences.i: For we know this well in our minds, and every one of you is a witness, all you whom the spirits of death have not carried off:
sentences.n: What follows is known to every survivor. ἴδμεν is the epic ἴσμεν ‘we know’, and τόδε points ahead to the omen. οὓς μὴ … ἔβαν is a relative clause with μή: ‘whom … did not’, that is, those spared. ἔβαν is the epic aorist of βαίνω, and ἔβαν … φέρουσαι ‘went bearing’ means ‘carried off’. κῆρες θανάτοιο are the ‘death-spirits’; κῆρες is a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
χθιζά τε καὶ πρωΐζ’ ὅτ’ ἐς Αὐλίδα νῆες Ἀχαιῶν
ἠγερέθοντο κακὰ Πριάμῳ καὶ Τρωσὶ φέρουσαι,
sentences.l:
yesterday and the day before, when to Aulis the ships of the Achaeans
were gathering, evils for Priam and the Trojans bearing,
sentences.i: yesterday and the day before, when the ships of the Achaeans were gathering at Aulis, bringing evils to Priam and the Trojans,
sentences.n: χθιζά τε καὶ πρωΐζ’ is ‘yesterday and the day before’, in effect ‘only the other day’, though nine years have passed. Αὐλίδα is the accusative of Αὐλίς, the harbour where the fleet gathered before sailing. ἠγερέθοντο is the imperfect of ἀγερέθομαι, a longer form of the middle ἀγείρομαι ‘gather’. κακὰ … φέρουσαι ‘bringing evils’ agrees with νῆες, the ships; Priam and the Trojans are the ones the evils are for.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἀμφὶ περὶ κρήνην ἱεροὺς κατὰ βωμοὺς
ἕρδομεν ἀθανάτοισι τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας
καλῇ ὑπὸ πλατανίστῳ ὅθεν ῥέεν ἀγλαὸν ὕδωρ·
sentences.i: and we, around a spring at the sacred altars, were sacrificing complete hecatombs to the immortals beneath a fair plane-tree, from which splendid water flowed;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ περὶ κρήνην ‘around a spring’ has two words for ‘around’, with κρήνην in the accusative; ἱεροὺς κατὰ βωμούς ‘at the sacred altars’. ἕρδομεν is the imperfect of ἕρδω ‘do, perform’, here ‘sacrifice’. τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας ‘complete hecatombs’, a large sacrifice. ὑπὸ πλατανίστῳ ‘beneath a plane-tree’. ὅθεν ῥέεν ἀγλαὸν ὕδωρ is ‘from where splendid water flowed’; ἀγλαός keeps the house rendering ‘splendid’ even for water.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα·
sentences.l: Then there appeared a great sign;
sentences.i: Then a great sign appeared:
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ‘then, there’ marks the moment. ἐφάνη is the aorist passive of φαίνω ‘show’, used as ‘appeared’; it keeps the augment. σῆμα ‘sign’ is a god-sent portent, and what it is comes in the next word, δράκων. Calchas will call it τέρας ‘portent’ at 324.

sentences.t:
δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινὸς
σμερδαλέος, τόν ῥ’ αὐτὸς Ὀλύμπιος ἧκε φόως δέ,
βωμοῦ ὑπαΐξας πρός ῥα πλατάνιστον ὄρουσεν.
sentences.l:
a serpent, blood-red on its back,
frightful, which the Olympian himself sent to the light,
from beneath the altar darting out, rushed at the plane-tree.
sentences.i: a serpent, blood-red along its back, frightful, which the Olympian himself had sent forth into the light, and which darted out from beneath the altar and rushed at the plane-tree.
sentences.n: δράκων ‘serpent’ stands in apposition to σῆμα. δαφοινός is usually taken as ‘blood-red’ (δα- an intensifier, φοινός ‘red’), but the sense is not certain; ‘tawny’ is another view. ἐπὶ νῶτα is ‘over the back’. αὐτὸς Ὀλύμπιος is ‘the Olympian himself’, Zeus, whom the speech does not name until 324. ἧκε φόως δέ: ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’, and φόως δέ is φόωσδε ‘to the light’, the suffix -δε of direction printed as a word, not ‘and light’. βωμοῦ ὑπαΐξας ‘darting out from under the altar’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔσαν στρουθοῖο νεοσσοί, νήπια τέκνα,
ὄζῳ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῳ πετάλοις ὑποπεπτηῶτες
ὀκτώ, ἀτὰρ μήτηρ ἐνάτη ἦν ἣ τέκε τέκνα·
sentences.i: And there were the nestlings of a sparrow, little children, crouching beneath the leaves on the topmost branch, eight of them; and the mother who bore the children was the ninth;
sentences.n: ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘there were’. στρουθός is a small bird, ‘sparrow’; νεοσσοί ‘nestlings’ and νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’ are in apposition, and the poet goes on calling the young birds ‘children’. ὄζῳ … ἀκροτάτῳ ‘on the topmost branch’. ὑποπεπτηῶτες is the perfect participle of ὑποπτήσσω ‘crouch’. Eight young and the mother as the ninth give nine birds. ἣ is the relative ‘who’; τέκε is unaugmented ‘bore’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε τοὺς ἐλεεινὰ κατήσθιε τετριγῶτας·
sentences.l: There he, for his part, was devouring them pitiably, as they cheeped;
sentences.i: There he was devouring them, as they cheeped pitiably;
sentences.n: ὅ γε is ‘he, for his part’, the serpent. κατήσθιε is the imperfect of κατεσθίω ‘eat up’, without the final -ν, ‘was devouring’. τετριγῶτας is the perfect participle of τρίζω ‘cheep, squeak’, the sound the young birds make. ἐλεεινά, a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘pitiably’, can go with κατήσθιε or with τετριγῶτας; the English puts it with the cheeping.

sentences.t: μήτηρ δ’ ἀμφεποτᾶτο ὀδυρομένη φίλα τέκνα·
sentences.l: and the mother fluttered around, lamenting her dear children;
sentences.i: and the mother fluttered about them, lamenting her dear children;
sentences.n: ἀμφεποτᾶτο is the contracted epic imperfect of ἀμφιποτάομαι ‘flutter around’. ὀδυρομένη is the participle of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’, here with an object: she mourns for her φίλα τέκνα ‘dear children’. The serpent has taken the brood; now it comes to the mother.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἐλελιξάμενος πτέρυγος λάβεν ἀμφιαχυῖαν.
sentences.l: and her, having coiled himself, by the wing he seized, as she shrieked around.
sentences.i: and, coiling himself, he seized her by the wing as she shrieked about them.
sentences.n: τὴν … λάβεν is ‘seized her’ (λάβεν is the unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω), and πτέρυγος in the genitive is the part taken hold of, ‘by the wing’. ἐλελιξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl, make quiver’; ‘coil himself’ is the sense taken from the scene. ἀμφιαχυῖαν is the perfect participle of ἀμφιάχω ‘cry around’; it is rare, and ‘shriek around’ is the sense taken from its formation and the scene.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ τέκνα φάγε στρουθοῖο καὶ αὐτήν,
τὸν μὲν ἀρίζηλον θῆκεν θεὸς ὅς περ ἔφηνε·
sentences.l:
But when he had eaten up the sparrow’s children, and her too,
him indeed conspicuous made the god, the very one who had shown him;
sentences.i: But when he had eaten up the sparrow’s children, and her too, the very god who had shown him made him conspicuous;
sentences.n: κατὰ … φάγε is tmesis for κατέφαγε ‘ate up’, unaugmented. στρουθοῖο is the genitive ‘of the sparrow’. τὸν μέν ‘that one’ is the serpent. ἀρίζηλον ‘very clear, conspicuous’ (ἀρι- is an intensifier) follows θῆκεν ‘made’ in a double accusative: ‘made him conspicuous’. θεὸς ὅς περ ἔφηνε is ‘the very god who had shown him’, the Olympian of 309; περ gives ὅς the sense ‘the very one who’.

sentences.t: λᾶαν γάρ μιν ἔθηκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω·
sentences.l: for a stone him made the son of Cronus of crooked cunning;
sentences.i: for the son of Cronus, of crooked cunning, made him a stone;
sentences.n: λᾶαν ‘stone’ (λᾶας; Attic λίθος) is the second accusative after ἔθηκε ‘made’, and μιν is ‘him’, the serpent. Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω is ‘the son of Cronus of crooked cunning’: πάϊς is παῖς, and the genitive ἀγκυλομήτεω agrees with Κρόνου, so the epithet is Cronus’. The god is at last named by his father, and at 324 by his own name.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δ’ ἑσταότες θαυμάζομεν οἷον ἐτύχθη.
sentences.l: and we, standing, marvel what sort of thing was made.
sentences.i: and we stood there marvelling at what had come about.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δ’ ‘but we’ goes back to the people at the altars. ἑσταότες is the epic perfect participle of ἵστημι, Attic ἑστῶτες ‘standing’. θαυμάζομεν is a present, ‘we marvel’, a vivid present in a past story; the English uses the past. οἷον ἐτύχθη is an indirect exclamation: ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω ‘make’, so ‘what a thing had been made’, that is, ‘had come about’.

sentences.t:
ὡς οὖν δεινὰ πέλωρα θεῶν εἰσῆλθ’ ἑκατόμβας,
Κάλχας δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα θεοπροπέων ἀγόρευε·
sentences.l:
So when the dread monsters of the gods came in upon the hecatombs,
Calchas at once then, prophesying, declared:
sentences.i: When the dread monsters of the gods had come in upon the hecatombs, Calchas at once declared, prophesying:
sentences.n: ὡς οὖν ‘so when’ picks the story up after the wonder of 320. δεινὰ πέλωρα is a neuter plural with the singular verb εἰσῆλθ’ (εἰσῆλθε): the portent as a whole, though the Greek says ‘monsters’. θεῶν could go with πέλωρα (‘the gods’ monsters’) or with ἑκατόμβας (‘the gods’ hecatombs’); the English keeps the Greek order. θεοπροπέων ἀγόρευε is ‘prophesying, declared’, ἀγορεύω being the verb of a public pronouncement.

sentences.t: τίπτ’ ἄνεῳ ἐγένεσθε κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί;
sentences.l: ‘Why ever have you become speechless, long-haired-of-head Achaeans?
sentences.i: ‘Why have you fallen speechless, long-haired Achaeans?
sentences.n: Calchas’ words as Odysseus remembers them, so the speech opens with a single quotation mark inside Odysseus’ speech. τίπτ’ is τίπτε ‘why ever’. ἄνεῳ is the nominative plural of ἄνεως ‘speechless’, and ἐγένεσθε the aorist ‘you became’; ‘fell speechless’ is the house rendering. κάρη κομόωντες ‘long-haired’ (κομάω ‘wear the hair long’; κάρη is κάρα ‘head’) is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, translated every time.
sentences.mark: Calchas speaks, as Odysseus tells it

sentences.t:
ἡμῖν μὲν τόδ’ ἔφηνε τέρας μέγα μητίετα Ζεὺς
ὄψιμον ὀψιτέλεστον, ὅου κλέος οὔ ποτ’ ὀλεῖται.
sentences.l:
To us this great portent showed counsellor Zeus,
late, late-fulfilled, whose fame will never perish.
sentences.i: Zeus the counsellor has shown us this great portent, a late one, late to be fulfilled, whose fame will never perish.
sentences.n: ἡμῖν μέν is ‘to us, for our part’. ἔφηνε is the aorist of φαίνω ‘showed’; τέρας μέγα ‘a great portent’. μητίετα Ζεύς ‘counsellor Zeus’ is a stock phrase, translated every time; μητίετα is an old nominative in -α (like ἱππότα at 336). ὄψιμον ὀψιτέλεστον: both words begin with ὀψ- ‘late’, and the pair says the sign is slow to come true. ὅου is the epic genitive of the relative (= οὗ) ‘whose’, and goes back to τέρας.

sentences.t:
ὡς οὗτος κατὰ τέκνα φάγε στρουθοῖο καὶ αὐτὴν
ὀκτώ, ἀτὰρ μήτηρ ἐνάτη ἦν ἣ τέκε τέκνα,
ὣς ἡμεῖς τοσσαῦτ’ ἔτεα πτολεμίξομεν αὖθι,
τῷ δεκάτῳ δὲ πόλιν αἱρήσομεν εὐρυάγυιαν.
sentences.l:
As this one ate up the sparrow’s children, and her too,
eight, but the mother was the ninth, who bore the children,
so we, so many years, shall fight here,
and in the tenth the wide-streeted city we shall take.’
sentences.i: As this one ate up the sparrow’s children, and her too, eight, and the mother who bore the children was the ninth, so we shall fight here for so many years, and in the tenth we shall take the city of the wide streets.’
sentences.n: Calchas reads the omen: each bird is a year. ὡς … ὣς ‘as … so’. οὗτος is ‘this one’, the serpent. Line 327 repeats 313 word for word, and the English repeats too; the first half of 326 echoes 317. τοσσαῦτ’ is τοσαῦτα with the epic double σ, ‘so many’, with ἔτεα (epic for ἔτη) ‘years’. πτολεμίξομεν is the epic form of πολεμίζω ‘fight’, read as a future, ‘we shall fight’. τῷ δεκάτῳ ‘in the tenth’ (year); αἱρήσομεν ‘we shall take’. εὐρυάγυιαν ‘of the wide streets’. The single closing mark ends Calchas’ speech.

sentences.t: κεῖνος τὼς ἀγόρευε·
sentences.l: That man thus was speaking;
sentences.i: That is how he spoke;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks again, with his own double quotation mark still open. κεῖνος is the epic ‘that man’ (= ἐκεῖνος), and ἀγόρευε an imperfect, ‘he was declaring’. τὼς is the adverb ‘thus, so’ (= ὥς, οὕτως), not a form of the article. The unit is the same Greek, and the same English, as a unit of the Odyssey.

sentences.t: τὰ δὴ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται.
sentences.l: these things now all are being fulfilled.
sentences.i: and now all of it is being fulfilled.
sentences.n: τά is the pronoun ‘these things’, with πάντα ‘all’ in apposition; δὴ νῦν ‘now indeed’. τελεῖται is the present passive of τελέω ‘fulfil’: Odysseus says the long wait is the omen working itself out. The Odyssey has this unit too, right after the one before it, and its English is followed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μίμνετε πάντες ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
αὐτοῦ εἰς ὅ κεν ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἕλωμεν.
sentences.l:
But come, stay, all of you, well-greaved Achaeans,
right here, until the great city of Priam we take.”
sentences.i: But come, stay here, all you well-greaved Achaeans, until we take Priam’s great city.”
sentences.n: Odysseus ends on a command. ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’; μίμνετε is the present imperative of μίμνω, the epic form of μένω ‘stay’; ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘right here, on the spot’, not a genitive. εἰς ὅ κεν with the subjunctive ἕλωμεν (aorist of αἱρέω) is ‘until we take’. The closing mark ends Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀργεῖοι δὲ μέγ’ ἴαχον, ἀμφὶ δὲ νῆες
σμερδαλέον κονάβησαν ἀϋσάντων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν,
μῦθον ἐπαινήσαντες Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Argives shouted loudly, approving the speech of divine Odysseus, and all around the ships rang frightfully at the shouting of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: The army answers. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’. Ἀργεῖοι and Ἀχαιῶν name one army, and the English keeps the poet’s two names. ἴαχον is the unaugmented aorist of ἰάχω ‘cry out’. κονάβησαν (κοναβέω ‘ring, resound’) has the adverb σμερδαλέον ‘frightfully’. ἀϋσάντων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘at the shouting of the Achaeans’, ὑπό with the genitive of cause. ἐπαινήσαντες is nominative, so it goes with Ἀργεῖοι: ‘approving’. θείοιο is ‘divine’.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: And among them the Gerenian horseman Nestor spoke up as well:
sentences.n: Nestor’s standing name and epithet, translated every time. The meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (Gerenia, a place in Messenia, or a link with γέρων ‘old man’ or γέρας ‘honour’), and no choice is made. ἱππότα is the old nominative of ἱππότης ‘horseman’. τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε ‘and among them spoke also’, μετέειπε the aorist of μετεῖπον in its epic form, with the vowel doubled (μετέειπε for μετεῖπε). Nestor’s speech begins on the next line.

sentences.t:
ὦ πόποι ἦ δὴ παισὶν ἐοικότες ἀγοράασθε
νηπιάχοις οἷς οὔ τι μέλει πολεμήϊα ἔργα.
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly, like children you speak in assembly,
childish ones, to whom the works of war are no care at all.
sentences.i: “Ah, truly, you hold forth in the assembly like children, childish creatures to whom the deeds of war are no concern.
sentences.n: Nestor opens with a rebuke. ὦ πόποι is ‘Ah!’. παισὶν ἐοικότες is ‘resembling children’ (ἔοικα with the dative); ἀγοράασθε is the diectasis form of ἀγορᾶσθε, from ἀγοράομαι ‘speak in the assembly’; νηπιάχοις ‘childish’ agrees with παισίν. οἷς οὔ τι μέλει is ‘to whom it is no care at all’, with πολεμήϊα ἔργα ‘the works of war’ as its subject. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: besides the usual shortening of ποι before ἦ, it scans only if the opening ἀ of ἀγοράασθε, short by nature, counts as long in the fifth foot.

sentences.t: πῇ δὴ συνθεσίαι τε καὶ ὅρκια βήσεται ἥμιν;
sentences.l: Where now will covenants and oaths go for us?
sentences.i: Where, now, will our covenants and oaths go?
sentences.n: πῇ δή ‘where, now?’ asks what will become of the army’s sworn agreements. συνθεσίαι ‘covenants’ (a συνθεσίη is a compact) and ὅρκια ‘oaths’ are the subject; βήσεται (the future of βαίνω ‘go’) is singular because it agrees with the nearer ὅρκια, a neuter plural. ἥμιν is the epic ἡμῖν ‘to us’. The question is rhetorical: Nestor means they are being treated as worth nothing.

sentences.t:
ἐν πυρὶ δὴ βουλαί τε γενοίατο μήδεά τ’ ἀνδρῶν
σπονδαί τ’ ἄκρητοι καὶ δεξιαί, ᾗς ἐπέπιθμεν·
sentences.l:
In the fire indeed may they be, plans and counsels of men,
and libations unmixed and right hands, in which we trusted;
sentences.i: Let them be in the fire, then, the plans and counsels of men, the unmixed libations and the right hands in which we trusted;
sentences.n: ἐν πυρὶ … γενοίατο is an optative of wish, ‘may they be in the fire’: a curse on everything that has not held. βουλαί ‘plans’ and μήδεα ‘counsels’ are near-synonyms. σπονδαί are libations poured to seal an agreement, ἄκρητοι ‘unmixed’ (neat wine), and δεξιαί ‘right hands’ the handclasps. ᾗς is a relative in the dative plural, ‘in which’, with ἐπέπιθμεν, the epic pluperfect of πείθομαι ‘trust’, used with the force of an imperfect, ‘we trusted’.

sentences.t:
αὔτως γὰρ ἐπέεσσ’ ἐριδαίνομεν, οὐδέ τι μῆχος
εὑρέμεναι δυνάμεσθα, πολὺν χρόνον ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντες.
sentences.l:
For just so with words we quarrel, and not any remedy
to find are we able, a long time here being.
sentences.i: For we are quarrelling with words to no purpose, and we can find no remedy, though we have been here so long.
sentences.n: αὔτως is ‘just so’, that is ‘idly, to no purpose’. ἐπέεσσ’ is ἐπέεσσι, the epic dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’. ἐριδαίνομεν ‘we quarrel’. οὐδέ τι μῆχος εὑρέμεναι δυνάμεσθα is the phrase of Odyssey 12.392: εὑρέμεναι is the epic infinitive of εὑρίσκω, δυνάμεσθα is δυνάμεθα ‘we are able’, and μῆχος is ‘remedy’. πολὺν χρόνον ‘for a long time’ is an accusative of duration, and ἐόντες the epic ‘being’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη σὺ δ’ ἔθ’ ὡς πρὶν ἔχων ἀστεμφέα βουλὴν
ἄρχευ’ Ἀργείοισι κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας,
τούσδε δ’ ἔα φθινύθειν ἕνα καὶ δύο, τοί κεν Ἀχαιῶν
νόσφιν βουλεύωσ’· ἄνυσις δ’ οὐκ ἔσσεται αὐτῶν·
sentences.l:
Atreus’-son, you, still as before holding an unshaken plan,
lead the Argives in the strong battles,
but let these waste away, one and two, who apart from the Achaeans
may plan; no accomplishment of them will there be;
sentences.i: Son of Atreus, hold to your unshaken plan as before, and lead the Argives through the strong battles; but let these men waste away, one or two, who plan apart from the Achaeans; there will be no accomplishment of what they plan;
sentences.n: Nestor turns to Agamemnon. ἄρχευ’ is an elided imperative, probably ἄρχευε, a by-form of ἄρχε from ἄρχω ‘lead’ (the formation is uncertain), with ἔθ’ ὡς πρίν ‘still as before’ and the participle ἔχων; ἀστεμφέα ‘unshaken’, of uncertain formation, goes with βουλήν ‘plan’. τούσδε ‘these men’ are those who would break away; ἔα, from ἐάω, is ‘let’, with φθινύθειν ‘waste away’. ἕνα καὶ δύο ‘one and two’ means a very few. τοί κεν … βουλεύωσ’ ‘who may plan’, νόσφιν Ἀχαιῶν ‘apart from the Achaeans’. ἄνυσις ‘accomplishment’; αὐτῶν ‘of them’ is taken as ‘of what they plan’.

sentences.t:
πρὶν Ἄργος δ’ ἰέναι πρὶν καὶ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
γνώμεναι εἴ τε ψεῦδος ὑπόσχεσις εἴ τε καὶ οὐκί.
sentences.l:
before to go to Argos, before also of aegis-bearing Zeus
to know whether the promise is a falsehood or else not.
sentences.i: before we go to Argos, before we learn whether the promise of aegis-bearing Zeus is a falsehood or not.
sentences.n: The two πρίν clauses depend on the sentence before: the plans of the dissidents will not succeed ‘before’ any of this. Ἄργος δ’ is Ἄργοσδε ‘to Argos’, the suffix -δε of direction printed as a separate word and elided. Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο belongs with ὑπόσχεσις in the next line; the meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed (usually ‘holding the aegis’). γνώμεναι is the epic infinitive (= γνῶναι) ‘to find out’. εἴ τε … εἴ τε καὶ οὐκί is ‘whether … or whether not’, with ψεῦδος ‘falsehood’ as predicate.

sentences.t:
φημὶ γὰρ οὖν κατανεῦσαι ὑπερμενέα Κρονίωνα
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε νηυσὶν ἐν ὠκυπόροισιν ἔβαινον
Ἀργεῖοι Τρώεσσι φόνον καὶ κῆρα φέροντες
ἀστράπτων ἐπιδέξι’ ἐναίσιμα σήματα φαίνων.
sentences.l:
For I say, then, that he nodded assent, the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength,
on that day when upon their swift-faring ships were embarking
the Argives, to the Trojans slaughter and doom bringing,
flashing lightning on the right, showing fitting signs.
sentences.i: For I say that the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength, nodded his assent on the day when the Argives were embarking on their swift-faring ships, bringing slaughter and doom to the Trojans: he flashed lightning on the right and showed fitting signs.
sentences.n: Nestor’s evidence that Zeus is on their side. Κρονίωνα is ‘the son of Cronus’, and κατανεῦσαι ‘nodded assent’, as in the nod of 1.528; ὑπερμενέα ‘of surpassing strength’. νηυσὶν ἐν … ἔβαινον is ‘were embarking on the ships’ (tmesis), νηυσὶν ὠκυπόροισιν ‘swift-faring ships’. φόνον καὶ κῆρα φέροντες ‘bringing slaughter and doom’. The participles ἀστράπτων and φαίνων belong to Zeus, though they are nominative where the infinitive construction would have the accusative. ἐπιδέξια ‘on the right’ was the lucky side for a sign. ἐναίσιμα ‘fitting’, from αἶσα ‘portion’, means of an omen ‘favourable’.

sentences.t:
τὼ μή τις πρὶν ἐπειγέσθω οἶκον δὲ νέεσθαι
πρίν τινα πὰρ Τρώων ἀλόχῳ κατακοιμηθῆναι,
τίσασθαι δ’ Ἑλένης ὁρμήματά τε στοναχάς τε.
sentences.l:
therefore let no one hasten before this to go home,
before someone beside a wife of the Trojans has lain down,
and taken vengeance for Helen’s strivings and groans.
sentences.i: So let no man hasten to go home before he has lain down beside a wife of the Trojans, and taken vengeance for Helen’s strivings and groans.
sentences.n: τὼ is ‘therefore’. ἐπειγέσθω is the third-person imperative of ἐπείγομαι ‘hasten’; οἶκον δέ νέεσθαι ‘to go home’ (δέ again the suffix -δε). πρίν τινα … κατακοιμηθῆναι is πρίν with an accusative and infinitive, ‘before someone has lain down’; the aorist passive of κατακοιμάω ‘put to sleep’, the plain sense being ‘to sleep with’. ὁρμήματα (ὁρμή ‘rush, impulse’) is ‘strivings’; whether they are Helen’s own efforts or the Achaeans’ efforts for her the Greek does not say. τίσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance for’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τις ἐκπάγλως ἐθέλει οἶκον δὲ νέεσθαι
ἁπτέσθω ἧς νηὸς ἐϋσσέλμοιο μελαίνης,
ὄφρα πρόσθ’ ἄλλων θάνατον καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ.
sentences.i: But if anyone is terribly eager to go home, let him lay a hand on his own well-benched black ship, so that before the rest he may meet death and his doom.
sentences.n: The other half of the warning: whoever wants to go home so badly may start by touching his ship, and be the first to die. ἐκπάγλως ‘terribly’ is the adverb of ἔκπαγλος. ἧς is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative. ἁπτέσθω (ἅπτομαι) takes the genitive νηός, ‘lay hold of’; ἐϋσσέλμοιο μελαίνης ‘well-benched, black’ are the stock epithets of a ship, translated every time. ἐπίσπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐφέπω ‘meet with’, after ὄφρα of purpose; πρόσθ’ ἄλλων ‘before the others’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ ἄναξ αὐτός τ’ εὖ μήδεο πείθεό τ’ ἄλλῳ·
sentences.l: But, lord, yourself take good thought, and be guided by another;
sentences.i: But, lord, take good thought yourself, and be guided by another;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ ἄναξ ‘but, lord’: ἄναξ is the vocative; Agamemnon is not called by his own name until 362. μήδεο and πείθεο are middle imperatives with the epic ending -εο (= -ου): μήδομαι ‘take thought’ and πείθομαι ‘be persuaded by, obey’, which takes the dative ἄλλῳ. Nestor asks Agamemnon to be guided by someone other than himself, and is about to offer his own advice.

sentences.t: οὔ τοι ἀπόβλητον ἔπος ἔσσεται ὅττί κεν εἴπω·
sentences.l: not to be thrown away, indeed, will the word be, whatever I say;
sentences.i: No word of mine will be one to throw away, whatever I say;
sentences.n: ἀπόβλητον is a verbal adjective of ἀποβάλλω ‘throw away’: ‘to be thrown away’. οὔ τοι … ἔσσεται ‘will not be’ (ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί); τοι is either ‘for you’ or the particle, and the English leaves it unsaid. ὅττί κεν εἴπω ‘whatever I may say’ is a subjunctive with κεν.

sentences.t:
κρῖν’ ἄνδρας κατὰ φῦλα κατὰ φρήτρας Ἀγάμεμνον,
ὡς φρήτρη φρήτρηφιν ἀρήγῃ, φῦλα δὲ φύλοις.
sentences.l:
Sort the men by tribes, by clans, Agamemnon,
so that clan may help clan, and tribes tribes.
sentences.i: Sort the men by tribes and by clans, Agamemnon, so that clan may help clan, and tribes help tribes.
sentences.n: κρῖν’ is κρῖνε, the imperative of κρίνω ‘separate, sort’. κατὰ φῦλα κατὰ φρήτρας is ‘by tribes, by clans’, κατά with the accusative meaning ‘by groups’: a φῦλον is a tribe and a φρήτρη a clan or brotherhood. ὡς with the subjunctive ἀρήγῃ is purpose, ‘so that … may help’. φρήτρηφιν is the dative of φρήτρη with the old suffix -φιν, and the verb is understood in φῦλα δὲ φύλοις. The point is that men should fight beside their own kin.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν ὣς ἕρξῃς καί τοι πείθωνται Ἀχαιοί,
γνώσῃ ἔπειθ’ ὅς θ’ ἡγεμόνων κακὸς ὅς τέ νυ λαῶν
ἠδ’ ὅς κ’ ἐσθλὸς ἔῃσι·
sentences.i: If you do this, and the Achaeans obey you, you will know then which of the leaders is base and which of the people, and which one is good;
sentences.n: εἰ … κεν with the aorist subjunctive ἕρξῃς (ἔρδω ‘do’) is a condition about the future, ‘if you do so’. καί τοι πείθωνται: τοι is ‘you’ (σοι), the dative with πείθωνται ‘obey’. γνώσῃ is the future of γιγνώσκω ‘come to know’. ὅς θ’ … ὅς τέ νυ … ἠδ’ ὅς κ’ lists three men: a bad leader, a bad follower, a good one. κακός and ἐσθλός are ‘base’ and ‘good’, here in battle. ἔῃσι is the epic subjunctive of εἰμί (= ᾖ).

sentences.t: κατὰ σφέας γὰρ μαχέονται.
sentences.l: for by themselves they will be fighting.
sentences.i: for they will be fighting each by themselves.
sentences.n: κατὰ σφέας γάρ gives the reason: once the men are sorted into tribes and clans, each body fights by itself and shows what it is. σφέας is the epic accusative plural of σφεῖς, ‘themselves’, and κατὰ σφέας ‘by themselves’. μαχέονται is from μαχέομαι (= μάχομαι), epic uncontracted, and can be read as a present or, as in Ionic, a future; the English takes the future because the sentence looks ahead.

sentences.t:
γνώσεαι δ’ εἰ καὶ θεσπεσίῃ πόλιν οὐκ ἀλαπάξεις,
ἦ ἀνδρῶν κακότητι καὶ ἀφραδίῃ πολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
And you will know whether indeed by a wondrous (power) the city you will not lay waste,
or through the baseness of men and folly in war.”
sentences.i: And you will know whether it is by some wondrous power that you will fail to lay waste the city, or through the baseness of men and their folly in war.”
sentences.n: Nestor names the two ways the city might not fall: the gods’ doing, or the army’s own fault. γνώσεαι is the uncontracted form of γνώσῃ (365). εἰ καί is ‘whether indeed’. θεσπεσίῃ ‘wondrous’ is a feminine dative with no noun; the Greek leaves it to the hearer, and the usual understanding is a divine ordinance, set against ἀνδρῶν κακότητι. οὐκ ἀλαπάξεις ‘you will not lay waste’. κακότητι ‘baseness’ is the noun of κακός, here the baseness of men in war; ἀφραδίῃ ‘folly’. The closing mark ends Nestor’s speech; Agamemnon answers at 2.369.
